div.head: Hn 72.3
div.ab: Qui non potest ieiunando peccata curare, potest elemosina redimere: elemosina sufficit sine ieiunio; ieiunium non sufficit sine elemosina.
div.note: New row (October 2026): Liebermann’s text transcribed from Gesetze I p. 590 (two independent readings of the page images, differences settled against the page)

note.seg: vielleicht rechtfertigt 72, 3 grundsätzlich die in Angelsächs. und Fränk. Kirche herrschende Redemtionspraxis (Wasserschleben 50; Schmitz 147 f. 237. 326), nach der es Tarife für Fasten gab, und scheint nicht Hn’s Eigen

perhaps 72, 3 justifies in principle the practice of redemption prevailing in the Anglo-Saxon and Frankish Church (Wasserschleben 50; Schmitz 147 f. 237. 326), under which there were tariffs for fasting, and it seems not to be Hn’s own
iei.—elem. fehlt K Co Or Gi [wohl wegen 72, 3a]
iei.—elem. missing in K Co Or Gi [probably because of 72, 3a]

Ein Prediger um 1000 in Agsächs. Sprache erklärt, Fasten (s. d. Gl 13) ohne Almosen sei nutzlos; ed. M. Förster in Morsbach Festschr. 82. Zugrunde liegt Vulgata Ecclesiasticus III 33: elemosyna resistit peccatis.—Am Rande spät: Peccatum curari posse elemosina absque ieiunio, et non e con[verso?]—72, 3b habeat{2} Rs

A preacher writing in Anglo-Saxon c. 1000 declares that fasting (see that word in Gl 13) without alms is useless; ed. M. Förster in Morsbach Festschr. 82. Underlying this is the Vulgate, Ecclesiasticus III 33: elemosyna resistit peccatis.—In the margin, in a late hand: Peccatum curari posse elemosina absque ieiunio, et non e con[verso?]—72, 3b habeat{2} Rs
